subject: biology

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the means of inheritance in eukaryotes that have a sexual life cycle?
items.correct: Each parent produces haploid gametes by meiosis, and their fusion forms a diploid zygote with two copies of each autosomal gene
items.misconception: Each parent's gametes carry both of its alleles of every gene, so the zygote's traits blend the two parental genotypes
items.why: Earlier courses speak of a child 'getting genes from both parents' without linking this to meiosis halving the chromosome number, and everyday talk of children as a 'mix' of their parents suggests whole genotypes are passed on and blended. Meiosis produces haploid gametes with one copy of each autosomal gene, so a parent passes only one of its two alleles of each gene, chosen at random. Fusion of two haploid gametes restores the diploid number: the zygote has two copies of each autosomal gene, one from each parent, and these remain separate alleles rather than blending.
items.specStatementText: Haploid gametes fuse to make a diploid zygote
items.random_wrong: Haploid gametes fusing to form a zygote is the pattern in animals, while plants pass on their genes through pollen and seeds instead

items.q: A breeder wants to cross a tall pea plant with a dwarf pea plant to obtain an F1 generation. Which procedure is required, and why?
items.correct: Remove the anthers from flowers of one plant, then transfer pollen from the other plant to their stigmas, because a pea flower would otherwise self-pollinate
items.misconception: Place pollen from one plant on the stigma of the other, where it fuses with the female gamete, so there is no need to remove the anthers first
items.why: Pollination is taught first and is often described as 'pollen fertilizes the flower'; pollen is the visible object transferred, so it is taken to be the gamete and the stigma, where it lands, is taken to be where the female gamete is. Pollen grains contain the male gametes but are not gametes themselves. The female gametes are in ovules inside the ovary, at the base of the carpel, so after pollination a pollen tube must grow down the style to deliver a male gamete to the ovary. Pollination is the transfer of pollen; fertilization is the later fusion of gametes.
items.specStatementText: How a plant cross is done
items.random_wrong: Grow the two plants next to each other, because a pea flower cannot be fertilized by its own pollen and so has to be cross-pollinated by insects

items.q: A pea plant has the genotype Tt for the gene controlling stem height. Which statement about this plant is correct?
items.correct: It is heterozygous, since it has two different alleles of one gene
items.misconception: It has two separate genes controlling stem height, called T and t
items.why: Everyday language and news reports say 'the gene for' a characteristic, and early courses often use 'gene' loosely for both the locus and its variants, so the distinction is never made explicit. All people have the same genes at the same loci; what differs between individuals is which alleles of each gene they carry. Blue and brown eye colour are due to different alleles of the same gene, not to different genes. A genotype is the combination of alleles inherited, and describing it as homozygous or heterozygous refers to whether the two alleles of one gene are the same or different.
items.random_wrong: It is heterozygous because its phenotype differs from both its parents

items.q: Which list gives a human trait due to genotype only, then a trait due to environment only, then a trait due to interaction between genotype and environment, in that order?
items.correct: ABO blood group; a scar; adult height
items.misconception: Adult height; a facial scar; skin colour
items.why: Genetics is taught through traits such as flower colour and blood group that are indeed set by genotype alone, and the Punnett grids predict phenotypes directly from genotypes, so the environment is never seen to enter the calculation. Phenotype is the set of observable traits resulting from genotype and environmental factors. Some human traits are due to genotype only (ABO blood group), some to environment only (scars, first language spoken), and many, such as height and skin colour, result from interaction: the genotype sets a range and the environment determines where within it the individual falls. Identical twins with the same genotype can differ in these traits.
items.random_wrong: ABO blood group; adult height; a facial scar

items.q: In peas the allele T for tall stems is dominant to the allele t for dwarf stems, and TT and Tt plants are equally tall. What is the reason that the heterozygote is not shorter than the homozygous dominant plant?
items.correct: One T allele makes enough functional protein for full stem growth, so the t allele has no observable effect
items.misconception: The T allele switches off the t allele in the heterozygote, so the plant effectively has two working T alleles
items.why: The word 'dominant' suggests an active contest in which the stronger allele wins, and diagrams that show only the phenotype of a heterozygote give no hint that the hidden allele is intact. Dominance is a matter of what the two alleles' products do, not of one allele suppressing the other. Typically the dominant allele codes for a functional protein and one copy makes enough of it, while the recessive allele codes for a non-functional or absent protein. The recessive allele remains in the heterozygote unchanged, is placed into half its gametes, and can produce the recessive phenotype in a homozygous recessive child.
items.specStatementText: Why one dominant allele is enough
items.random_wrong: Tall plants are more common than dwarf plants, so the tall allele is the stronger one and takes over

items.q: A person's skin darkens after several weeks in strong sunlight and returns to its previous colour over the winter. How is this change best explained?
items.correct: Phenotypic plasticity: sunlight alters the expression of genes for melanin production, and the change reverses because the genotype is unchanged
items.misconception: It is phenotypic plasticity: ultraviolet light causes mutations in the melanin genes, which produce extra pigment until the mutations are repaired in winter
items.why: Students learn that traits come from genes, so a new trait seems to require new genes; and 'the environment affects the phenotype' is easily misheard as 'the environment affects the genotype'. Phenotypic plasticity is the capacity to develop traits suited to the environment experienced, by varying patterns of gene expression. Different genes are switched on or off, or expressed to different extents, in response to environmental signals, while the base sequences of the alleles remain exactly as they were inherited.
items.specStatementText: Phenotypic plasticity: adjusting without changing genes
items.random_wrong: It is an adaptation acquired during life, and because it is adaptive it will be permanent and passed on to the person's children

items.q: PKU usually appears in a child whose parents are both unaffected. Which statement correctly describes phenylketonuria (PKU)?
items.correct: It is caused by a recessive allele of an autosomal gene coding for the enzyme that converts phenylalanine to tyrosine
items.misconception: It is caused by a dominant allele of an autosomal gene, which is why the condition is expressed in every person who carries it
items.why: The name contains 'phenyl' and the treatment is a low-phenylalanine diet, so students conclude the problem is phenylalanine itself rather than the missing enzyme; and because the condition is expressed in the affected person, they assume the allele must be dominant. PKU is a recessive genetic condition caused by mutation in an autosomal gene that codes for the enzyme needed to convert phenylalanine to tyrosine. Two mutant alleles are needed for the disease because one functional allele gives enough enzyme. Phenylalanine from the diet cannot be converted and builds up, which is why the diet is restricted; the affected person makes too little tyrosine from phenylalanine, not too little phenylalanine.
items.random_wrong: It is caused by a recessive allele that prevents the body making phenylalanine, so affected people need extra phenylalanine in their diet

items.q: A man and a woman are both unaffected carriers of the PKU allele. They already have one child with PKU. What is the probability that their next child will have PKU?
items.why: Students reason quantitatively that one allele should give half the effect of two, and the term 'carrier' suggests someone who has the condition in some diminished form. For a trait with complete dominance, one functional allele produces enough functional protein to give the full dominant phenotype, so the homozygous-dominant and heterozygous genotypes produce the same phenotype. Carriers of recessive conditions such as PKU are phenotypically unaffected. An intermediate phenotype in the heterozygote is the separate pattern called incomplete dominance.

items.q: A gene in a human population has eleven known alleles, which differ from one another at single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Which statement is correct?
items.correct: All eleven alleles can exist in the gene pool, but any one individual inherits at most two of them
items.misconception: Only two of the eleven can be true alleles, one dominant and one recessive; the rest must be alleles of other genes
items.why: Introductory crosses use one dominant and one recessive allele written as a capital and a lower-case letter, and a diploid individual has two alleles, so 'two' becomes the number of alleles a gene has rather than the number an individual carries. Mutation can produce new alleles at any time, so a gene may have many alleles in a population's gene pool, such as the three ABO alleles or the hundreds of alleles of some human genes. A diploid individual still inherits only two of them, one from each parent, and the relationship between those two need not be simple dominance.
items.specStatementText: Many alleles in the gene pool, two in each person
items.random_wrong: An individual can carry several of the eleven alleles at once, since each SNP creates a separate copy of the gene

items.q: A woman with blood group A whose genotype is IAi has children with a man of blood group B whose genotype is IBi. Which blood groups are possible in their children, and with what probabilities?
items.correct: Groups AB, A, B and O are all possible, each with a probability of 1 in 4
items.misconception: Groups A, B and AB, each 1 in 3, but not group O, as neither parent is group O
items.why: Blood group is treated as a trait passed down as a unit, and the recessive i allele, having no visible effect in the parents, is forgotten. Blood group phenotypes A and B can each be produced by a heterozygous genotype carrying the recessive allele i. A cross IAi × IBi gives IAIB (AB), IAi (A), IBi (B) and ii (O), each with a probability of 1 in 4, so every ABO blood group is possible among the children.
items.random_wrong: Groups A and AB only, each 1 in 2, because the IA allele is dominant to IB

items.q: In the four o'clock plant Mirabilis jalapa, a cross between a red-flowered plant and a white-flowered plant gives only pink-flowered offspring. Two of these pink plants are crossed. What phenotypes are expected in their offspring?
items.correct: Red, pink and white flowers in a 1:2:1 ratio, as both alleles persist
items.misconception: Pink only, because the red and white alleles have merged into a pink allele
items.why: The intermediate phenotype looks exactly like a mixture of paints, and the pre-Mendelian idea of blending inheritance matches this everyday intuition. Incomplete dominance affects the phenotype, not the alleles. Each pink heterozygote produces red-allele and white-allele gametes in equal numbers, so pink × pink gives 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, recovering the parental phenotypes. Alleles are inherited as discrete units and do not blend.
items.random_wrong: Pink and white in a 3:1 ratio, because pink is dominant to white

items.q: In the ABO system the red blood cells of a person with genotype IAIB carry both the A antigen and the B antigen. In Mirabilis jalapa a heterozygote for the flower-colour alleles has pink petals. What do these observations show about the two patterns of inheritance?
items.correct: Blood group AB is codominance, since both alleles are fully expressed together; pink is incomplete dominance, since the heterozygote is intermediate
items.misconception: Both are examples of the same pattern, in which the alleles are mixed in the heterozygote, so AB and pink are both intermediate phenotypes
items.why: Both patterns are exceptions to complete dominance in which the heterozygote looks different from both homozygotes, and both are often illustrated with flower colour, so the two are filed together as 'blending'. The prefix 'co-' also suggests co-operation to produce a blend, so students attach 'codominance' to the intermediate phenotype. The patterns differ at the phenotypic level. In codominance both alleles are fully expressed side by side, as in blood group AB, where both A and B antigens are present. In incomplete dominance neither allele is fully dominant and the heterozygote is intermediate, as in the pink flowers of Mirabilis jalapa. Pink is not red and white together; AB is not a blend of A and B.
items.random_wrong: Blood group AB shows that IA is dominant to IB, while pink petals show that the red allele is dominant to the white allele

items.q: Which statement about sex determination and the sex chromosomes in humans is correct?
items.correct: The sex chromosome carried by the sperm determines the sex of the zygote, and the X chromosome carries far more genes than the Y
items.misconception: The sex chromosome carried by the egg determines the sex of the zygote, and the X chromosome carries far more genes than the Y does
items.why: The mother carries and gives birth to the child, so she is assumed to determine its characteristics; and students who know that both parents contribute a sex chromosome conclude that both contribute to the decision. A female is XX and produces only X-carrying eggs. A male is XY and produces X-carrying and Y-carrying sperm in equal numbers. It is therefore the sex chromosome in the sperm that determines whether the zygote develops male-typical or female-typical physical characteristics.
items.random_wrong: The sex chromosome carried by the sperm determines the sex of the zygote, and the X and Y chromosomes carry the same genes

items.q: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia (XHXh) has children with a man who does not have haemophilia (XHY). Their first child is a boy. What is the probability that he has haemophilia?
items.why: Ratios are first met as exact outcomes (a Punnett grid with four cells is read as four children), and students have no feel for independent events, so they expect the ratio to be filled in like a quota and apply it to any group of children without recalculating. A Punnett grid gives the probability for each fertilization. Each child of two carriers has a 1 in 4 chance of PKU regardless of previous children, and a family may have any number of affected children. When a question restricts attention to a subgroup, such as sons, the probability must be recalculated for that subgroup.

items.q: Why is haemophilia far more common in males than in females?
items.correct: Males have one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele produces the condition, whereas a female needs two
items.misconception: The allele is carried on the Y chromosome, so that a father passes the condition directly to each one of his sons
items.why: Students expect sex-specific characteristics to pass from father to son, and the fact that haemophilia is much more common in males is misread as father-to-son transmission. The haemophilia allele is on the X chromosome (Xh). A father gives his X chromosome to every daughter and his Y to every son, so an affected father (XhY) has carrier daughters (XHXh) and unaffected sons. A son can inherit haemophilia only from his mother's X chromosome.
items.random_wrong: Females who inherit the allele can only ever be carriers, because the female body cannot develop the condition

items.q: A man and a woman who are both unaffected by a genetic disorder have three children: an affected daughter, an unaffected son and an unaffected daughter. The affected daughter later has four children with an unaffected man, and all four are unaffected. What can be deduced about the disorder?
items.correct: It is autosomal recessive, and both parents of the affected daughter must be heterozygous carriers
items.misconception: It is autosomal dominant, because the daughter shows the disorder while her parents are merely carriers
items.why: Students associate 'appears' with 'dominant' and treat any disorder that misses a generation as unusual and therefore sex-linked, without applying the rule that unaffected parents can only pass on a hidden, recessive allele. A dominant disorder is shown by every individual who carries the allele, so an affected child would have at least one affected parent. Unaffected parents producing an affected child is the signature of a recessive allele carried by both. Whether it is autosomal or X-linked is decided by the sexes involved: an affected daughter must have received a recessive X-linked allele from her father, so if he is unaffected the gene is autosomal.
items.specStatementText: Reading a pedigree, and inductive versus deductive reasoning
items.random_wrong: It is X-linked recessive, since the disorder skipped a generation and none of the affected daughter's children show it

items.q: Many societies prohibit marriage between close relatives. What is the genetic basis for this prohibition?
items.correct: Close relatives are more likely to carry the same recessive allele inherited from a common ancestor, so their children are more likely to be homozygous for it
items.misconception: Reproduction between close relatives causes new mutations, producing genetic disorders that were not present in the family beforehand
items.why: The harm is well known but its mechanism is not taught early, so students supply the most familiar cause of genetic damage, mutation, rather than reasoning about the sharing of existing alleles. No new mutation is involved. Everyone carries some recessive disease alleles that are harmless in a heterozygote. Two unrelated partners rarely carry the same one, but two relatives may both have inherited it from a shared grandparent, so their child has a raised chance of receiving it from both sides. This is the genetic basis for the prohibition of marriage between close relatives in many societies.
items.specStatementText: Reading a pedigree, and inductive versus deductive reasoning
items.random_wrong: Recessive alleles that were switched off in each parent become active again when the same allele arrives from both sides of the family

items.q: Human skin colour varies continuously across a population, whereas ABO blood group falls into four separate classes. Which explanation of this difference is correct?
items.correct: Skin colour depends on several genes and on sunlight, giving many grades; blood group depends on one gene with discrete alleles
items.misconception: Skin colour is controlled by one gene with a very large number of alleles, whereas the blood group gene has only three alleles
items.why: Multiple alleles and polygenic inheritance are both met as 'more than two' and are confused, and sun-tanning is so visible that some students credit the environment with all the variation. A single gene, however many alleles it has in the gene pool, gives each individual at most two alleles and so a small number of phenotypes. Continuous variation needs many genes each adding a small effect, which produces many combinations, and environmental factors then blur the classes further. Skin colour has both components.
items.random_wrong: Skin colour is determined by the environment only, with no genetic contribution, whereas blood group is determined by genotype only

items.q: The heights in centimetres of nine students are: 150, 152, 152, 155, 158, 160, 163, 170 and 175. What are the mean, median and mode of these heights?
items.correct: Mean 159.4 cm, median 158 cm, mode 152 cm
items.misconception: Mean 158 cm, median 159.4 cm, and mode 152 cm
items.why: The three words are learned together as 'averages', and in symmetrical textbook data sets they coincide, so students do not register that they are calculated differently. Mean, median and mode are different measures of central tendency and can take different values for the same data. The mean uses every value and is pulled towards outliers; the median is the value in the middle when the data are ordered; the mode is the most common value. For a skewed set of heights all three can differ.
items.random_wrong: Mean of 159.4 cm, median 152 cm, mode 158 cm

items.q: For a class's heights, the first quartile is 150 cm, the median is 158 cm, the third quartile is 166 cm, and the minimum and maximum are 130 cm and 192 cm. Above what height would a data point be categorized as an outlier on a box-and-whisker plot?
items.correct: 190 cm
items.misconception: 182 cm
items.why: The median is the reference point students know best, and in many plots the whiskers reach the extremes, so the extremes and outliers are not distinguished. The 1.5 × IQR rule is measured from the quartiles, not the median: the upper limit is Q3 + 1.5 × IQR and the lower limit is Q1 − 1.5 × IQR. Only values beyond these limits are outliers and plotted as separate points; the whiskers end at the most extreme values that are not outliers.
items.random_wrong: 174 cm

items.q: A plant is heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes (AaBb). Which event in meiosis determines which allele of the first gene ends up in a gamete together with which allele of the second gene?
items.correct: The random orientation of each bivalent on the equator at metaphase I, which is independent of the orientation of the other bivalent
items.misconception: Crossing over between the two genes during prophase I, which exchanges alleles between chromosomes to make the four combinations
items.why: Students learn the names of meiotic stages separately from Mendelian ratios, and the most memorable events (crossing over, chromatid separation) are assumed to be the ones that shuffle alleles. Independent assortment results from the random orientation of bivalents in metaphase I: which homologue of one pair faces a given pole has no effect on the orientation of any other pair. Segregation of alleles follows in anaphase I. This produces all four gamete types from a double heterozygote in equal proportions, which is the basis of the 9:3:3:1 ratio for unlinked genes.
items.specStatementText: Segregation and independent assortment come from meiosis
items.random_wrong: The separation of sister chromatids at anaphase II, which sends the two alleles of each gene into two different gametes

items.q: Two pea plants heterozygous for two unlinked genes (RrYy) are crossed. Why is the expected phenotypic ratio among their offspring 9:3:3:1?
items.correct: Each gene independently gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive, and multiplying the probabilities gives 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 for the four phenotype combinations
items.misconception: The 16 cells of the Punnett grid contain four genotypes in the proportions 9:3:3:1, and each of these genotypes gives a different phenotype
items.why: In a monohybrid cross the three genotypes map neatly onto the 3:1 ratio, so students expect the dihybrid ratio to be a genotypic one as well and do not count the 16 cells of the Punnett grid by genotype. The 16 cells of a dihybrid Punnett grid contain nine different genotypes; the 9:3:3:1 ratio arises only when these are grouped by phenotype (both dominant traits, 9; one dominant and one recessive, 3 each; both recessive, 1). The 9 class contains four genotypes (AABB, AABb, AaBB and AaBb).
items.random_wrong: Each parent makes four types of gamete and these combine with the single gamete type of the other parent in equal numbers, giving 9:3:3:1

items.q: Mendel's second law predicts a 9:3:3:1 ratio in the F2 of a dihybrid cross, yet a cross involving two genes close together on the same chromosome gives a ratio far from this. What does this show about the law?
items.correct: The law applies only when genes are on different chromosomes or far enough apart to recombine freely; all biological laws have exceptions
items.misconception: The law is universal, so the unexpected ratio must be the result of new mutations or of errors made in scoring the offspring
items.why: 9:3:3:1 is the ratio students memorise for 'dihybrid', so it is applied regardless of the parents' genotypes, and Mendel's laws are presented as laws with no conditions attached. The ratio depends on the parents. AaBb × AaBb combines four gamete types from each parent to give 9:3:3:1; AaBb × aabb combines four gamete types with a single ab gamete to give 1:1:1:1. Both derive from Mendel's second law, which applies only if the genes are on different chromosomes or far enough apart on one chromosome for recombination to reach 50%; linked genes give different ratios, an example of the exceptions that all biological laws have under certain conditions.
items.random_wrong: The law still applies because all genes assort independently; the unexpected ratio must arise from unequal survival of the different offspring

items.q: In a genome database, a student finds that a human gene has its locus on chromosome 11 and that a second gene has its locus a few thousand base pairs away on the same chromosome; each record names a different polypeptide product. Which conclusion is correct?
items.correct: The two genes are linked, because their loci are in close proximity on the same chromosome, and each codes for its own polypeptide
items.misconception: The two records must describe alleles of one gene, because different sequences at nearby positions are alternative forms of the same gene
items.why: Alleles are drawn as differently coloured blocks and described as 'different forms', which suggests different places; and students who have seen that chromosome number varies between species assume gene position varies between people. A locus is the specific position of a gene on a particular chromosome, recorded in genome databases with the chromosome number and coordinates and with the polypeptide the gene codes for. All alleles of a gene occupy the same locus on the homologous chromosomes. Two genes may have loci on different chromosomes or in close proximity on the same chromosome, which determines whether they are linked.
items.random_wrong: The two genes are not linked, because gene linkage applies only to genes that are carried on the X chromosome

items.q: In a fruit fly the loci for body colour and wing shape are on the same autosome. A fly inherited one chromosome carrying the alleles G and W and the homologous chromosome carrying g and w, shown as G W and g w beside two vertical lines. Why does this fly not produce GW, Gw, gW and gw gametes in equal numbers?
items.correct: The alleles on each chromosome are passed on together unless crossing over between the loci separates them, which occurs in only some meioses
items.misconception: The two genes are permanently joined together on the chromosome, so only GW and gw gametes can ever be formed by this fly
items.why: 'Linked' suggests a fixed connection, and crossing over is taught as a source of variation without being connected to linkage; alternatively Mendel's second law is remembered as universal. Alleles of linked genes usually travel together because they are on the same DNA molecule, which is why the parental combinations dominate the offspring. Crossing over between the loci exchanges segments between non-sister chromatids and produces recombinant gametes, so recombinants appear but at less than 50%. Independent assortment applies only to genes on different chromosomes.
items.random_wrong: Because the genes are linked they must be on the X chromosome, so only female flies are able to produce the recombinant gametes

items.q: A fly heterozygous for two linked genes (AaBb), which inherited the alleles A and B on one chromosome and a and b on the other, is test-crossed with an aabb fly. The offspring are 42 AaBb, 38 aabb, 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb. Which offspring are the recombinants, and what produced them?
items.correct: The 11 Aabb and 9 aaBb, produced by crossing over between the two loci in the heterozygous parent
items.misconception: The 42 AaBb and 38 aabb, because these offspring differ in genotype from the homozygous recessive parent
items.why: 'Recombinant' is heard as 'different from the parents' in the everyday sense, and crossing over is described as occurring in every meiosis, which suggests recombinant gametes are the norm. Recombinant gametes, genotypes and phenotypes are those with new combinations of alleles relative to the two parental chromosomes of the heterozygote (for example Ab and aB when the parent was AB/ab). Crossing over between two particular loci happens in only some meioses, so for linked genes recombinants are the minority classes; for unlinked genes they equal the parental classes at 50%.
items.specStatementText: Spotting recombinants in a test cross
items.random_wrong: None of them, because two genes that are linked cannot give rise to any new combinations of their alleles

items.q: A cross between two double heterozygotes gives 160 F2 offspring: 95 show both dominant traits, 28 show the first dominant and the second recessive, 30 show the first recessive and the second dominant, and 7 show both recessive traits. The critical value of chi-squared at p = 0.05 is 7.815 for 3 degrees of freedom and 9.488 for 4 degrees of freedom. What is the outcome of a chi-squared test against a 9:3:3:1 ratio?
items.correct: Expected numbers are 90, 30, 30 and 10; chi-squared is about 1.3, below 7.815, so the null hypothesis is not rejected and the data fit 9:3:3:1
items.misconception: Expected numbers are 90, 30, 30 and 10; chi-squared is about 1.3, below 7.815, so the difference is significant and the two genes are linked
items.why: In most school measures a bigger number means a better result, so a large chi-squared is taken as a good fit; and 'not rejecting' the null hypothesis is naturally but wrongly upgraded to 'proving' it. Chi-squared measures the discrepancy between observed and expected numbers, so a large value means a poor fit. If chi-squared is greater than the critical value, the probability of the discrepancy arising by chance is less than 0.05 and the null hypothesis is rejected. If it is smaller, the data are consistent with the expected ratio; the null hypothesis is retained but not proved.
items.specStatementText: Chi-squared: do the numbers fit the ratio?
items.random_wrong: Expected numbers are 9, 3, 3 and 1; chi-squared is far above 9.488 for 4 degrees of freedom, so the null hypothesis must be rejected

items.q: A student carries out a chi-squared test on the F2 offspring of a dihybrid cross. Which statement about the test is correct?
items.correct: The null hypothesis is that observed and expected numbers do not differ significantly, and the F2 counted is a sample of the population
items.misconception: The null hypothesis is that the two genes are linked, so that the observed numbers will differ from those expected from the predicted ratio
items.why: Students expect the hypothesis under test to be the interesting claim, and 'null' is not linked to 'no difference'. The null hypothesis states there is no difference beyond chance between observed and expected results; for a dihybrid cross this means the genes assort independently and the 9:3:3:1 or 1:1:1:1 ratio holds. The alternative hypothesis states that there is a significant difference. The test decides whether the sample, here the F2 generation, gives enough evidence to reject the null hypothesis.
items.specStatementText: Chi-squared: do the numbers fit the ratio?
items.random_wrong: If the calculated chi-squared value is below the critical value at p = 0.05, the null hypothesis has been proved to be true

items.q: Which organisms inherit their genes through haploid gametes fusing to form a diploid zygote?
items.correct: All eukaryotes with a sexual life cycle, including plants and fungi as well as animals.
items.misconception: Only animals produce gametes and zygotes; plants reproduce by seeds and pollen, which are something different from gametes.
items.why: Gametes are introduced through human sperm and eggs, and plant reproduction is taught in terms of pollen, seeds and flowers, so the two are filed as unrelated processes rather than the same haploid–diploid cycle. Production of haploid gametes and their fusion to form a diploid zygote is the means of inheritance in all eukaryotes with a sexual life cycle. In flowering plants the male gametes are inside the pollen grains and the female gametes are in the ovules within the ovary; their fusion forms a diploid zygote that develops into the embryo inside the seed.
items.specStatementText: Haploid gametes fuse to make a diploid zygote
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many alleles of an autosomal gene does a diploid body cell contain?
items.correct: Two: one on each of the pair of homologous chromosomes, one inherited from each parent.
items.misconception: A body cell has a single copy of each gene, so a person 'has' one allele for each trait and passes that allele to each child.
items.why: Genes are named as if they were single objects ('the gene for eye colour'), and diagrams of a chromosome show a gene as one band, so the existence of a second copy on the homologous chromosome is easy to overlook. A diploid cell has two copies of each autosomal gene because it has two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent. The two copies may be the same allele (homozygous) or different alleles (heterozygous), and meiosis places only one of them in each gamete.
items.specStatementText: Haploid gametes fuse to make a diploid zygote
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a single pea plant be both parents of its own offspring?
items.correct: Yes. Peas produce both male and female gametes on the same plant, so a flower can self-pollinate and then self-fertilize.
items.misconception: A genetic cross always needs two separate plants, because an organism cannot fertilize itself.
items.why: Animals, the familiar example, have separate sexes, so students carry the assumption that reproduction requires two individuals over to plants. The word 'cross' also suggests two different parents. Plants such as peas produce both male and female gametes on the same plant, allowing self-pollination and therefore self-fertilization. This is why the F2 generation can be produced simply by letting F1 plants self-pollinate, and why a breeder must remove the anthers from a flower to prevent selfing when a cross between two different plants is required.
items.specStatementText: How a plant cross is done

items.q: What are the P, F1 and F2 generations in a genetic cross?
items.correct: The P generation is the pair of parents first crossed, the F1 generation is their offspring, and the F2 generation is the offspring produced when F1 individuals are crossed with each other or self-fertilized.
items.misconception: The F2 generation is produced by crossing F1 offspring back to the original P parents, or the F1 is simply the first cross and the F2 the second cross of the same parents.
items.why: The labels F1 and F2 look like a numbering of crosses rather than of generations, and students who have not seen a full two-generation cross worked through do not realise that the F2 comes from the F1 alone. P, F1 and F2 name successive generations: P are the original parents, F1 their offspring, and F2 the offspring of the F1. The 3:1 ratio of a monohybrid cross appears in the F2 because heterozygous F1 plants are crossed with each other or allowed to self-fertilize, not because they are crossed with the P generation.
items.specStatementText: How a plant cross is done
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does it mean for an organism to be heterozygous for a gene?
items.correct: It has two different alleles of that gene, one on each homologous chromosome.
items.misconception: Heterozygous means having two different genes for a trait, or that the organism differs from its parents, while homozygous means being the same as a parent.
items.why: 'Hetero' and 'homo' are learned as 'different' and 'same' without the object being specified, so students attach them to the nearest idea (genes, parents, siblings) rather than to the two alleles of one gene. Homozygous and heterozygous describe the two alleles of a single gene in a diploid organism: homozygous means the two alleles are the same (TT or tt), heterozygous means they are different (Tt). The terms say nothing about how many genes are involved or about resemblance to parents.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a trait caused only by the environment, such as a scar or a learned language, be inherited by offspring?
items.correct: No. Environment-only traits do not change the genotype, so they are not passed on through gametes.
items.misconception: Any characteristic an individual has, including ones acquired during life, is part of its phenotype and so can be passed to its children.
items.why: Phenotype is defined as 'observable traits', and inheritance is described as passing on traits, so students join the two and expect any observable trait, however it arose, to be heritable. Only the genotype is transmitted through gametes. A trait due to the environment only, such as a scar, a suntan or the language a person speaks, is part of that individual's phenotype but has no basis in the alleles inherited, so it cannot be passed to offspring. Suggesting examples of traits due to genotype only, environment only, and interaction of the two makes this distinction clear.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is it decided which allele of a gene is dominant?
items.correct: By the phenotype of the heterozygote: the allele whose effect appears in the heterozygote is dominant. Dominance has nothing to do with how common the allele or the phenotype is.
items.misconception: The dominant allele is the more common, stronger or 'better' one, so the phenotype seen in most of a population must be the dominant phenotype.
items.why: The everyday meaning of 'dominant' is 'prevailing' or 'most powerful', and in textbook crosses the dominant phenotype does happen to be the more frequent one in the F2, so frequency and dominance become fused. Dominant and recessive describe the relationship between two alleles in a heterozygote, not their frequency or value. Many dominant alleles are rare (for example the allele causing polydactyly) and many recessive alleles are common. Only a cross or pedigree in which the heterozygote's phenotype can be seen reveals which allele is dominant.
items.specStatementText: Why one dominant allele is enough
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a trait produced by phenotypic plasticity permanent, and can it be inherited by the organism's offspring?
items.correct: It may be reversible during the individual's lifetime if the environment changes, and because the genotype is unchanged it is not inherited through the gametes.
items.misconception: Once an organism has adapted its phenotype to its environment the change is permanent, and because it is an adaptation it will be passed on to the offspring.
items.why: 'Adaptation' is used in evolution for inherited features shaped by natural selection, so students assume that any adaptive change in an individual is likewise fixed and heritable. Changes due to phenotypic plasticity are not due to changes in genotype, and they may be reversible: a suntan fades, and muscle built by training is lost when training stops. Because the alleles are unchanged, the plastic trait itself is not transmitted to offspring, although the capacity for plasticity is inherited.
items.specStatementText: Phenotypic plasticity: adjusting without changing genes
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is a single-nucleotide polymorphism, and how many alleles of a gene can one person carry?
items.correct: A SNP is a position in the genome at which a single nucleotide varies between individuals in a population; it is the commonest way alleles differ. A person carries at most two alleles of any autosomal gene, whatever the number in the gene pool.
items.misconception: A SNP is any mutation that changes a whole gene, and because a gene can have many alleles an individual can carry several of them at once.
items.why: Students link 'polymorphism' with 'many forms' and 'multiple alleles' with 'multiple in one person', and the scale of a SNP (a single base out of billions) is hard to picture against diagrams that show whole genes as coloured blocks. A SNP is variation at one nucleotide position; two alleles of a gene may differ by a single SNP or by several. Multiple alleles exist in the gene pool because different SNPs and other mutations have arisen in different lineages, but each diploid individual has only two copies of the locus and so at most two different alleles.
items.specStatementText: Many alleles in the gene pool, two in each person
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the dominance relationship between the alleles IA, IB and i?
items.correct: IA and IB are codominant with each other, and both are dominant to i.
items.misconception: IA is dominant to IB (or the reverse), or the i allele is dominant, so a person with genotype IAIB has group A and a person with IAi has group O.
items.why: Students expect every pair of alleles to fit the dominant/recessive pattern learned first, and the capital I in IA and IB alongside lower-case i is read as a simple two-level hierarchy rather than a three-allele system. The ABO gene has three alleles. IA and IB each code for an enzyme that adds a different antigen to red blood cells; in the heterozygote IAIB both are expressed, giving group AB (codominance). The i allele produces no antigen, so it is recessive to both: IAi is group A, IBi is group B and only ii is group O.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How does the number of genes on the Y chromosome compare with the number on the X chromosome?
items.correct: The X chromosome carries far more genes than the Y chromosome, which is much smaller and carries relatively few genes.
items.misconception: The X and Y chromosomes are a matching pair with the same genes, like the autosome pairs, so each X-linked gene has a partner allele on the Y.
items.why: Homologous chromosomes are taught as matching pairs carrying the same genes, and X and Y are drawn as a pair in karyotypes, so students assume they are homologous along their whole length. The Y chromosome is much smaller than the X and carries far fewer genes. Most genes on the X chromosome have no counterpart on the Y, so a male has only one copy of those genes. This is why recessive alleles of X-linked genes are expressed in males whenever present.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a female have haemophilia, and is a carrier female affected?
items.correct: A female can have haemophilia only if she is XhXh, which is rare; a heterozygous carrier XHXh is unaffected because the dominant allele on her other X chromosome provides the clotting factor.
items.misconception: Females cannot have haemophilia at all, or, conversely, a carrier female has a mild form of the condition and passes it to all her sons.
items.why: Sex-linked disorders are introduced as 'diseases of males', and the term carrier is taken to imply a partially affected state, so the two halves of the misconception come from the same source. Haemophilia is recessive, so it appears in a female only when both X chromosomes carry Xh, which requires an affected father and a carrier or affected mother. A carrier (XHXh) has one dominant allele and normal clotting. Each of her sons has a 1 in 2 chance of receiving Xh and having haemophilia, not a certainty.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is deducing a pattern of inheritance from a pedigree inductive or deductive reasoning?
items.correct: Inductive: a general conclusion (the disorder is autosomal recessive) is drawn from observations of some cases. Using that conclusion to work out the genotype of a specific individual is then deductive.
items.misconception: Working out the genotypes of individuals is inductive because it uses the observed pedigree, and generalising about the pattern of inheritance is deductive because it produces a theory.
items.why: The two words are unfamiliar and both processes use the pedigree, so students attach 'deductive' to the step that sounds like detective work and 'inductive' to whatever remains. Inductive reasoning moves from particular observations to a general conclusion, and scientists use it when they base a theory on some but not all cases. Deductive reasoning applies a general principle to a specific case. In pedigree analysis, inferring the mode of inheritance from the observed pattern is inductive; predicting a named individual's genotype from that mode is deductive.
items.specStatementText: Reading a pedigree, and inductive versus deductive reasoning
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is ABO blood group a continuous or a discrete variable?
items.correct: Discrete: there are four separate groups with no intermediates.
items.misconception: Blood group is continuous because there are several categories, and height is discrete because it is measured to the nearest centimetre.
items.why: Students judge by the number of categories or by how the data are recorded, rather than by whether intermediate values are possible. A discrete variable falls into distinct categories with no intermediates, such as ABO blood group, whatever the number of categories. A continuous variable can take any value within a range, such as height or skin colour, even if it is recorded to a fixed precision. The distinction determines how the data are displayed and which statistics are appropriate.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does the box in a box-and-whisker plot represent?
items.correct: The interquartile range, from the first quartile to the third quartile, containing the middle half of the data, with a line marking the median.
items.misconception: The box shows the full range of the data from minimum to maximum, or it shows the mean plus and minus one standard deviation.
items.why: Students meet range and standard deviation as the measures of spread before quartiles, and error bars on bar charts look similar, so the box is read as one of those. The box spans Q1 to Q3, so its length is the IQR; the median, not the mean, is the line inside it. The whiskers show the minimum and maximum non-outlier values, and outliers are plotted separately. The IQR, not the range, is used in the outlier rule.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the alleles of two different genes that a parent inherited together stay together in its gametes?
items.correct: Not if the genes are unlinked: independent assortment means an AaBb parent produces AB, Ab, aB and ab gametes in equal proportions regardless of which combinations it inherited.
items.misconception: The alleles a parent received from its own mother stay together and go into one gamete, and those from its father go into another, so a dihybrid behaves like a monohybrid with only two gamete types.
items.why: The parental origin of chromosomes is emphasised when meiosis is first taught, and drawings usually colour all maternal chromosomes one colour, suggesting they move as a set. Each bivalent orients independently at metaphase I, so a gamete receives a random mixture of maternal and paternal chromosomes. For two unlinked genes the double heterozygote therefore produces four gamete types in equal numbers, not two. Only linked genes on the same chromosome tend to stay together, and even then crossing over produces recombinants.
items.specStatementText: Segregation and independent assortment come from meiosis
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What does it mean for two genes to be linked?
items.correct: Their loci are on the same chromosome, so their alleles tend to be inherited together. Autosomal linkage involves genes on the same autosome and is different from sex linkage.
items.misconception: Linked genes are genes on the sex chromosomes, so linkage and sex linkage are the same thing.
items.why: Sex linkage is met first and is the only 'linkage' many students have named, so the word is attached to the X chromosome rather than to the general idea of loci on the same chromosome. Gene linkage means two loci are on the same chromosome. When that chromosome is an autosome the genes are autosomally linked and their inheritance is unrelated to sex. Sex linkage refers to a single gene located on a sex chromosome. In crosses involving linkage, allele symbols are shown alongside vertical lines representing the homologous chromosomes to show which alleles are together.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How are the expected numbers and the degrees of freedom obtained for a chi-squared test on a dihybrid cross?
items.correct: The expected numbers are the total number of offspring divided in the predicted ratio (for example 9/16, 3/16, 3/16 and 1/16 of the total); the degrees of freedom are the number of phenotype classes minus one, so 3 for four classes.
items.misconception: The expected values are the observed values rounded to the nearest ratio, or the expected ratio itself (9, 3, 3, 1) is used directly; and the degrees of freedom equal the number of classes.
items.why: The ratio 9:3:3:1 is written with small numbers that look like counts, and 'degrees of freedom' is an unexplained label that students set equal to the most obvious number, the number of categories. Expected numbers must be scaled to the same total as the observed sample: with 160 offspring and a 9:3:3:1 ratio they are 90, 30, 30 and 10. Degrees of freedom are one fewer than the number of classes, because once the total is fixed only that many class sizes are free to vary; for four classes the critical value at p = 0.05 is read from the row for 3 degrees of freedom.
items.specStatementText: Chi-squared: do the numbers fit the ratio?
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
